title: Per Cent Unpacker
context: Grade 5, the page on per cents as fractions and decimals. An adult sees division by a hundred. What the page is doing is running the per cent backwards: a per cent is a number of hundredths, so it is written over 100 and simplified, or written as hundredths in decimal form. A per cent with a point becomes thousandths, and nothing here goes to a fourth place.

writeup.why: Write a per cent as a fraction in lowest terms, including per cents above one whole and below one per cent, and as a decimal through hundredths, or thousandths when it has a point.
writeup.look: A per cent card, its fraction over 100 and a bar under it at the left, and a hundred grid over a place value chart of ones, tenths, hundredths and thousandths at the right.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Per Cent Unpacker' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of hundredths the per cent names. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The per cent card stands at x 110, y 230, 200 by 90, deep blue, and the fraction over one hundred is written beside it at x 340, y 230. The bar under both lies at x 110, y 340, 600 long and 50 tall, keeping its shaded length whatever the terms become. When Divide by HCF is tapped the words Both terms light vermilion, and the fraction reached in lowest terms is green. The hundred grid, 300 by 300, stands at x 800, y 210, and on the second phase a second grid of the same size joins at x 450, y 420, under the bar. The place value chart stands under the first grid at x 800, y 530, 300 by 180, with four columns headed Ones, Tenths, Hundredths and Thousandths; an empty place holds a grey 0, and the decimal read off it is green. The Over 100, Divide by HCF, Hundredths and Split hundredths buttons stand in a column at x 110, y 420, each labelled in words. On the fourth phase each hundredth of the grid is cut into ten thin slices, each one thousandth. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a point key, a fraction bar key and a % key. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the tools of this chapter share them. The part the question gives, as shaded cells, a fraction, a decimal or an amount, is deep blue, labelled Given. The per cent, fraction or decimal the working reaches, and what is left after a part is used, is green, labelled Answer or Left. Both terms multiplied or divided by one number, and the times one hundred step before the % sign, are vermilion, labelled Both terms or Times 100. A unit fact that puts two amounts in one unit is violet, labelled Unit fact. The part used, taken away or not won is rose, labelled Used or Not won. The step, cell or number being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a decimal is grey, labelled Place holder, and nothing else on the stage is ever grey. An unshaded cell of a whole stays warm white inside its near-black outline, the % sign is near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The cards show the last per cent beside its fraction in lowest terms and its decimal, with the grid and the chart under them.

writeup.delight: On the fourth phase, each hundredth splits into ten thin slices with a soft ripple along the row, and the Thousandths column of the chart lights up for the first time.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet written. On the first phase the per cent card sits at the top left with the Over 100 button lit. On the second two cards wait, one above one hundred per cent over two grids and one below one per cent. On the third the per cent card sits over one grid and the chart is empty. On the fourth the card shows a per cent with a point, with some cells and part of one more shaded. One thing moves, once: the Over 100 button, or the Split hundredths button on the fourth phase, gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: A per cent of the child's own, written over 100 and simplified, poured into the chart or split into thousandths. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on lowest terms, per cents above one whole and below one per cent, and per cents as decimals.

source_tool.description: A per cent card stands at the top left of the working area, deep blue. An Over 100 button writes it as a fraction over 100 beside it, and a Divide by HCF button divides both terms by their HCF, lighting the words Both terms vermilion, while a bar 600 long under the fraction keeps its shaded length. The fraction reached in lowest terms is green. A hundred grid, 300 by 300, at the right of the working area shades the per cent as hundredths, with a second grid added for each whole. A place value chart of four columns, Ones, Tenths, Hundredths and Thousandths, stands under the grid; a Hundredths button pours the count into it, each empty place holding a grey 0, and the decimal is read off it in green. On the last phase a Split hundredths button cuts each hundredth into ten thin slices, each one thousandth. A number pad types a per cent, a fraction or a decimal. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of hundredths the per cent names.
source_tool.art_direction: Place value chart on a notebook page / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: hundred grids of ten rows and ten columns, strips cut into equal cells, fraction bars with their denominator of one hundred built beside them, measuring jugs, tapes and scales with their units written on them.

Every whole is drawn the same size as every other whole it is compared with, and its parts are exactly equal: a strip of ten has ten cells of one width, and a hundred grid is always a full ten by ten.
A whole is always labelled 100%, so the child sees what one hundred per cent means before any part is named.
Where shaded cells are counted, exactly the stated number is shaded, and they stay countable at a glance: full columns of ten first, then single cells.
A product that becomes a per cent is always written with its brackets, and the % sign comes last. A decimal reaches a per cent through its hundredths, never by moving anything.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: cells filling a grid, both terms of a fraction growing together, a unit fact rewriting an amount, or a used part lifting away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a cell or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a per cent plays in a piece of working: the part the question gives, as shaded cells, a fraction, a decimal or an amount, is deep blue, and the per cent, fraction or decimal the working reaches, with what is left after a part is used, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Both terms multiplied or divided by one number, and the times one hundred step before the % sign, are vermilion. A unit fact that puts two amounts in one unit is violet. The part used, taken away or not won is rose. The step, cell or number being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a decimal is grey. An unshaded cell of a whole stays warm white inside its outline, and the % sign itself is near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Both terms, Unit fact, Used, Not won, Left and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Write it over a hundred again, then look for the HCF.
voice.onNext: A new per cent. How many hundredths does it name?
voice.opening: A per cent, ready to be written over a hundred.
voice.onFinish: Every per cent went back to hundredths, then to its new form.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Unpack any per cent you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Very large and very small per cents

placement.where: After the class has written a few per cents over a hundred by hand and simplified them. The tool is what pours the hundredths into the chart and cuts a hundredth into ten, which paper can only draw finished.

answer_key.rule: A per cent is a number of hundredths. Write it over 100, then divide both terms by the HCF to reach lowest terms. A per cent above 100 is more than one whole, and its fraction is improper. A fraction of one per cent is that fraction of one hundredth: 1/2% is 1/2 x 1/100. A whole-number per cent is written as that many hundredths in decimal form. A per cent with one place after its point is read as thousandths, with three places after the point, and nothing here needs a fourth place. In a matching list, a pair that would need a fourth place after the point is found as the pair left over.
answer_key.wrong: The per cent is shaded again on the grid beside the child's answer, turned back into hundredths, so the two amounts are seen side by side, and the step where they part is lit amber. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

items.question: Write 36% as a fraction in lowest terms.
items.checkpoint: Write the per cent over 100, then divide both terms by the HCF.
items.misconception: Stopping at 18/50, which is simpler but not yet in lowest terms.

steps: Divide both terms by 20: 240/100 = 12/5, which is 2 2/5.
It is more than one whole, because 240% is more than one hundred per cent.
items.question: Write 240% as a fraction in lowest terms.
items.checkpoint: A per cent above one hundred gives a fraction more than one whole.
items.misconception: Writing 240/1, which forgets that per cent means out of a hundred.

steps: 83 hundredths is written 0.83: 8 tenths and 3 hundredths.
items.question: Write 83% as a decimal.
items.checkpoint: Write the per cent over 100, then write that many hundredths as a decimal.
items.misconception: Writing 8.3, which counts 83 tenths instead of 83 hundredths.

steps: Each hundredth is 10 thousandths, so 6.5 hundredths is 65 thousandths.
That is three places after the point, with 0 holding the tenths place.
items.question: Write 6.5% as a decimal.
items.checkpoint: A per cent with one place after its point becomes thousandths, three places after the point.
items.misconception: Writing 0.65, which is 65 hundredths, ten times too much.

teaching_notes: Write a few per cents over a hundred by hand before the tool opens, and simplify them by the HCF. Say per cent means out of a hundred each time. A per cent above one hundred is more than one whole. Read a whole-number per cent as hundredths to write its decimal, and a per cent with one place after its point as thousandths. Keep to three places after the point: in a matching list, a pair that would need a fourth place is found as the pair left over. Use fresh per cents: the exercise's own are the child's to convert.
generation_prompt: Build a per cent to fraction and decimal tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A per cent card stands at the top left. An Over 100 button writes it as a fraction over 100, and a Divide by HCF button divides both terms by their HCF, lighting the words Both terms vermilion, while a bar 600 long under the fraction keeps its shaded length; the lowest terms fraction is green. A hundred grid, 300 by 300, shades the per cent as hundredths, a grid for each whole. Under it a place value chart of four columns, Ones, Tenths, Hundredths and Thousandths, takes the count when a Hundredths button is tapped, with a grey 0 in each empty place. On the last phase a Split hundredths button cuts each hundredth into ten thin slices, each one thousandth. A number pad types per cents, fractions and decimals. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of hundredths. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
